adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Chile - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Chile country overview is the national framework a visitor to Región de Valparaíso stands under: the 2012 Zamudio anti-discrimination law protects sexual orientation and gender identity, civil unions have been recognised since 2015, and same-sex marriage with full adoption rights has been legal since March 2022. Gender Identity Law 21.120 (introduced 2013, enacted 2018) has since 2019 let transgender people aged 14 and over change their name and gender on all official documents without surgery, and the armed forces admit LGBT personnel. Until 2022 Article 365 of the Penal Code set a higher age of consent of 18 for male homosexual acts; the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in a 5-5 vote in August 2018, and it was abolished by Law 21,483 in August 2022, equalising the age of consent.

adds.title: Diversidad sexual en Chile - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
adds.summary: Spanish Wikipedia's overview of sexual diversity in Chile carries four items directly relevant to this region: the first Encuentro de Oficinas Municipales de Diversidad (gathering of municipal diversity offices) was held in 2022 in Valparaíso (the second in 2023 in Melipilla, the third in 2024 in Concepción); San Antonio, in Región de Valparaíso, was among the founding comunas of the Red de Municipalidades por la Diversidad, Inclusión y No Discriminación ('Red Diversa') created in 2014, a network of municipalities with LGBTIQA+ offices or programmes that had grown beyond 60 municipalities by 2024; in April 2016 the first Carabinero contracted a civil union with a same-sex partner; and in 2020 the Chilean Army formally incorporated its first transgender member. The same page confirms the national baseline: Ley Zamudio (2012) against discrimination, same-sex marriage under Ley 21.400 (promulgated 9 December 2021, in force 10 March 2022), and Ley 21.430 (2022) banning discrimination based on sex characteristics for children and adolescents.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Colombia overview is the national framework every visitor to Bogotá Capital District stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016 (making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so); adoption equality came in 2015; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; and transgender people have had a right to change legal gender recognised since 1993, reinforced by a 2012 Constitutional Court ruling allowing civil-registry change without a family court. It also records Bogotá-specific facts: a 2012 ruling let a transgender woman choose her own hairstyle and makeup in prison, Claudia López Hernández became the first openly gay person to serve as mayor of Bogotá, pride parades in Bogotá number among the country's large LGBTQ events, and a Washington Post report describes thriving gay neighbourhoods in Bogotá. Beginning in 2026, nonbinary and transgender options are offered on the national identity card.

adds.title: Diversidad sexual en Colombia - Wikipedia, la enciclopedia libre
adds.summary: Spanish Wikipedia's Colombia overview confirms the national baseline a Bogotá visitor stands under: in November 2015 the Constitutional Court approved adoption by same-sex couples and in April 2016 it approved same-sex marriage; the current documentation framework recognises four identity markers - female (F), male (M), trans (T) and non-binary (NB); and rulings T-033 of 2022 and T-527 of 2024 protected the right to gender identity and its recording. Despite the anti-discrimination laws, the page notes that prejudice and discrimination against LGBTI people remain present in a considerable part of the population - context relevant to a visibly gender-nonconforming person in central Bogotá.
